title: The kb plugin, capture, freshness and PR comments

story: Nova picks up a backend ticket: add a progress field to the message the cloud sends to on-prem clients. Before it plans, it should know the rule that protects the clients already installed at customers, and that rule is written in one brain page out of 35. Pasting all 35 pages into every prompt would make every run pay for pages about CI and releases that have nothing to do with the ticket, and the pile grows every week. So Nova has to find the one page that matters.

Then a teammate reviews the plan. It says: add the new field, and never rename the old one, because installed clients still read it. The reviewer has one question: says who? If the plan only says "the brain says so", she cannot check the claim, and the page may have changed since Nova read it.
hook.question: How does an agent find the one page it needs, and how can a reviewer check exactly what it read?

read.h: One small tool for every reader
p: The brain is read through one command, kb, with three subcommands: kb search finds pages, kb show prints one, and kb propose opens a pull request with a fix. It ships as a Claude Code plugin, so people get it with one install: the plugin's bin/ folder is on the PATH while the plugin is on, and a skill tells Claude when to use it. Nova uses the same command. Its kb_search tool in the harness (written in TypeScript) simply runs kb search as a process, so the command line is also the border between our TypeScript platform and the brain's Python tools.

kb search reads a local copy of rnd-kb, called a mirror: ~/.cache/rnd-kb on a laptop, or the folder in $KB_DIR inside an agent VM. When the mirror is more than an hour old, it runs git pull --ff-only first. The search code uses only Python's standard library on purpose: the CLI, Nova, the brain's test suite and the Slack bot all import the same file, so they rank pages in exactly the same way without installing anything.

read.h: Ranking by the words that matter
p: To rank pages, kb search uses BM25 (short for "Best Match 25"), a scoring formula search engines have used since the 1990s. It is worth understanding, because its three ideas explain most of its results. First, a page that contains a word from the question scores higher, but the tenth mention adds much less than the first, so repeating a word cannot win on its own. Second, rare words count more than common ones: "proto" appears in one page, "the" in every page, so a match on "proto" is worth far more. That weight is the IDF (inverse document frequency). Third, long pages are scored down a little, so a long page does not win just because it contains more words.

For Nova's question, "what must I check before I change a proto", the page about keeping installed clients working wins because it is the only page that says proto. No model call, no vector database, and the same answer every time. An agent is also a patient search user: when the first query misses, it tries another with better words, so a simple, predictable ranking works well for it.

notes.text: The two usual settings: K1 controls how fast repeats stop counting, B how much long pages are scored down.
df: in how many pages each word appears. Rare words have a small df.
The IDF: big for a word in one page, close to zero for a word in every page.
More mentions help, but less and less, and a long page needs more mentions for the same score.

p: Every result is printed as rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>, followed by the title, the effective confidence and the reviewed date. The sha is the commit of the mirror at the moment of the search. That small detail answers the reviewer's question. With git show <sha>:<path>, they open exactly the text Nova read, even if the page has changed since, and they can see whether Nova read a checked page or a draft.

The confidence in the line is the same effective confidence you met with the schema, so an old page announces itself as low wherever it appears. Agents treat such a page as a lead: a reason to look in the code, not a fact to repeat.

p: A search tool is useless if nobody calls it at the right moment. The kb skill is the label Claude reads in every session: its description says when the brain helps, and its body, loaded only when the skill is used, says how to use it well. Two lines in it matter most. "Search it even when you feel sure", because a model is most dangerous when it is confident about something our code does differently. And "if the brain has no answer, say so", because an agent that fills a gap from memory produces exactly the confident mistakes the brain exists to prevent.

code.text:
---
name: kb
description: "Use when you need to know how part of Rhino's system works, why it was built
  that way, or what was decided. Searches the R&D brain (RhinoHealth/rnd-kb), answers with
  citations as path@sha, and proposes a fix when a page is wrong."
when_to_use: "Questions like 'how does a code run reach the on-prem client?' or 'why does
  cloud CI run on push?'. Also before planning a change in an area you don't know well."
allowed-tools: Bash(kb search *) Bash(kb show *) Read
---
# kb: the R&D brain

The brain holds reasons and decisions the code doesn't show, so search it even when you feel sure.

1. `kb search "<question>"`; add `--path <file>` when you are about to change that file.
   Read the top pages with `kb show <path>`.
2. Weigh each page by its confidence and reviewed date. `low` or overdue means a lead,
   not a fact: confirm it in the code before you rely on it.
3. Cite each claim as `rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>`, exactly as the search prints it.
4. If the brain has no answer, say so plainly and say where you looked.
5. If a page is wrong: people run `kb propose <path>`; agents add it to the PR's
   "harness suggestions" section instead.

notes.text: The description is what Claude reads in every session to decide whether to open the skill.
Only the search and show commands, plus Read. The skill cannot write anything.
The rule that turns a confident guess into a lead.
Agents never open pull requests to the brain themselves; they report the problem in their own PR.

p: Search is only as good as the pages, so three small tools keep them current. /kb-capture is a second skill in the plugin that only a person can start (disable-model-invocation: true): it turns a PR discussion or a pasted Slack thread into a draft page at confidence: low, follows the data scope (summaries only from private channels, no customer names), and opens a pull request for the page's owner.

kb freshness runs every Monday from a workflow in rnd-kb and sends each owner one Slack message listing their overdue pages. And a small workflow in fcp compares each pull request's changed files with the applies_to globs in the brain's index.json, then posts or updates one comment listing the pages and owners to check. It is information only, never a required check, and it posts nothing when no page matches, because the cheapest moment to fix a page is while the author still remembers the change.

lab.title: A search that cites
lab.goal: Build a small BM25 search over a git mirror of brain pages that prints each hit as rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>, and boost the pages that describe the file you are about to change.

guess.q: The question is "what must I check before I change a proto". Five pages; "proto" appears only in the page about installed clients, and "what" appears in two others. Which page does BM25 put first?

options.text: The page that uses the most words from the question
options.why: Counting words treats "what" and "proto" the same. BM25 weighs each word by how rare it is.

options.text: The page about keeping installed clients working, because "proto" is rare
options.why: A word that appears in one page has a high IDF, so that one match outweighs common words elsewhere.

options.text: The longest page, because it has the most chances to match
options.why: BM25 scores long pages down a little for exactly this reason.

reviewed: 2026-10-14

# How a code run reaches the on-prem client
The on-prem client opens one outbound gRPC stream to the cloud; the cloud never connects in.
Work for the client, such as a code run, travels down that stream to the client's handlers.
EOF

---
title: Keeping installed on-prem clients working
confidence: med
reviewed: 2026-09-02
review_every: 90d
applies_to:
  - fcp:common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc/*.proto
---
# Keeping installed on-prem clients working
Clients installed at customers update months after the cloud. A proto is a contract with them:
add new fields, never rename or remove old ones, and regenerate the _pb2 files with make protoc.
EOF

title: Which CI workflow runs what, and when

---
title: Integration tests wait for the QA lock
confidence: high
reviewed: 2026-10-16
review_every: 90d

# Integration tests wait for the QA lock
There is one lock per component per cloud. A run waits until the lock for its component is free.
EOF
cat > rnd-kb/product/release-process.md <<'EOF'
---
title: How a release reaches the customers
confidence: med
reviewed: 2025-01-10
review_every: 90d
---
# How a release reaches the customers
The release is cut from main and the notes are written by the team that owns the change. Then the
release goes to the staging cloud, and the team checks that the release works there. Then the release
goes to the production cloud, and the customers get the release when the client is updated by the
customer. The notes go to the customers with the release, and the team answers the questions.
EOF

check.q: The question is "why does the client open the connection". "the" is in every page and "connection" in one. Which word decides the ranking most?

options.why: A word in every page has an IDF close to zero, so it barely moves any score.

options.text: "connection", because it is rare across the pages
options.why: Rare words carry the IDF weight. One match on "connection" outweighs any number of matches on "the".

options.text: All words count the same in BM25
options.why: That is plain word counting. BM25's IDF is exactly what makes words count differently.

check.q: Nova's plan cites rnd-kb/engineering/cloud-client-compatibility.md@3fa91c2. The page has changed twice since then. How does the reviewer check the claim?

options.text: Read the current page, because it is newer and better
options.why: The current page may say something Nova never read. The question is whether Nova used its source correctly.

options.text: Open git show 3fa91c2:engineering/cloud-client-compatibility.md and compare the claim with that text
options.why: The sha pins the exact version Nova read. If the page has changed since, that is a separate question for the plan.

options.text: Ask Nova to read the page again
options.why: Nova's new reading would be of a different version. The citation already says which text to check.

check.q: kb search returns a page labelled (low, reviewed 2025-01-10). What should Nova do with it?

options.text: Ignore it, because low pages are wrong
options.why: Low means not checked recently, not wrong. It is often the best lead available.

options.text: Use it as a fact, because it ranked first
options.why: Ranking says the words match. It says nothing about whether the page is still true.

options.text: Treat it as a lead: confirm the claim in the code before relying on it, and cite it
options.why: That is the skill's rule. A low or overdue page tells Nova where to look, and the code decides.

p: The kb plugin lives in rnd-kb-tooling/plugin/: .claude-plugin/plugin.json (name kb), skills/kb/SKILL.md, and bin/kb, a stdlib-only launcher that runs kb_tools/search.py shipped inside the plugin. kb search keeps the mirror (~/.cache/rnd-kb, or $KB_DIR in agent VMs), pulls with --ff-only when it is over an hour old, reads index.json, ranks with BM25 over title, headings and body, boosts --path matches on applies_to, and prints the top 5 as rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>  title  (effective confidence, reviewed). kb show prints a page with its sha; kb propose pushes a branch and opens a PR with gh, for people only. Five eval cases in plugin/evals/ check that it fires, cites, admits not knowing, treats an overdue page as a lead and stays quiet on unrelated requests. Platform lists the plugin in claude-plugins pinned by sha and bakes the CLI and a mirror into the agent image; the harness's kb_search runs this CLI.

/kb-capture (disable-model-invocation: true) turns a PR (gh pr view --comments) or a pasted thread into a low-confidence draft and runs kb lint and kb propose. kb freshness posts one Slack message per owner from rnd-kb's freshness.yml (cron 17 6 * * 1, SLACK_BOT_TOKEN of the "Rhino Brain" app with only chat:write, two weeks in --dry-run first). fcp's kb-pages.yml runs kb touched --index index.json --files changed.txt with the rhino-kb App token and edits one PR comment in place; it is never a required check, and Nova reads it as a hint.

tickets.why: The kb plugin: the CLI with search, show and propose, BM25 with path@sha citations, the skill and its evals.
/kb-capture: a PR or a Slack thread becomes a draft page for its owner.
kb freshness: a weekly Slack digest of overdue pages per owner.
kb touched and the fcp workflow that comments on PRs touching described code.

words.plain: A local git clone of rnd-kb that kb search reads and refreshes when it is more than an hour old.
A classic ranking formula: matching words help less with each repeat, rare words count more, long pages are scored down a little.
Inverse document frequency: the weight that makes a word found in few pages count more than one found in all of them.
rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>: the page and the exact commit it was read at, so anyone can open the same text.
The skill that tells Claude when to search the brain, how to weigh confidence, and to cite or say it does not know.

review.q: Explain BM25's three ideas in one sentence each.
review.a: Repeats of a word help less and less; rare words count more than common ones (IDF); long pages are scored down a little so length alone does not win.

review.q: Why does a citation carry the sha and not only the path?
review.a: Pages change. The sha lets anyone open exactly the text the agent read with git show <sha>:<path>, even after the page was edited.

review.q: What does --path add to a search, and where does the information come from?
review.a: It boosts pages whose applies_to globs match the file about to be changed, using the frontmatter of each page, so the page about that code comes first even when the question is vague.

remember: Find the one page with a simple, predictable ranking, and cite it as rnd-kb/<path>@<sha> so anyone can open exactly what was read.
